title: What even is cognitive activation?
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman examines the OECD's PISA category of 'cognitive activation', which is sometimes cited as evidence that effective teaching involves more than explicit instruction. He notes that the OECD does not ask the same questions consistently across PISA rounds, and that the 2025 report links cognitive activation to inquiry-based teaching even though earlier rounds found a negative association between inquiry learning and science scores. Digging into a spreadsheet at the back of the report, he lists the five questions behind the index and the adjusted association of each with PISA science scores. Three of the five, connecting new and old topics, memorising facts and explaining a principle, describe exactly what interactive explicit teaching looks like. The one item that really resembles inquiry, explaining how to design an experiment, shows no statistically significant association with achievement. Ashman concludes that a good foundation of knowledge is probably the best preparation, even for PISA's complicated, context-heavy questions.
points: The OECD does not consistently ask the same student-experience questions across PISA rounds, which makes trends in teaching styles hard to interpret.

Cognitive activation sounds more like a prerequisite for learning than a teaching style, yet it is treated as distinct from teacher-directed instruction and sometimes used to argue explicit teaching is not enough.
Three of the five items in the index, connecting old and new topics, memorising facts and explaining a principle, describe interactive explicit teaching in practice.

The inquiry-like item, explaining how to design an experiment, is the only one with no significant link to science achievement, which undercuts the OECD's claim that cognitive activation overlaps with inquiry.
Ashman argues that a solid knowledge base is likely better preparation for PISA's applied questions than anything else.
quotes: Through these questions, the OECD have identified different teaching styles. Three of these are ‘teacher-directed’, ‘student-oriented’ and ‘cognitive activation’. That third category is weird. It sounds more like a prerequisite for learning than a teaching style.

Indeed, in their PISA 2025 report, the OECD authors claim that, ‘In science, [cognitive activation] practices overlap with inquiry-based teaching, where students are encouraged to ask questions, formulate hypotheses, interpret evidence and reflect on conclusions’. That’s quite something given that they previously found a negative association between inquiry learning and PISA science scores.

Buried in an excel sheet in the basement of the latest PISA report is a table showing the different questions the OECD asked to create its index of cognitive activation and the association between each question and performance on the science PISA assessment.
What do you notice? Questions 1, 3 and 4 are exactly what you might expect to see in a class driven by interactive explicit teaching.

Given all the noise about memorisation in previous rounds of PISA—there was a Scientific American article on the woes of memorisation in maths that I criticised many moons ago—I find it surprising both that this sits in a definition of ‘cognitive activation’ and that this finding has passed unremarked by the OECD.

The question that is making up the numbers, with no statistically significant association with achievement, is the one about asking students to explain how they would design an experiment. Oddly enough, this would seem to be the one most relevant to PISA science questions.
Even so, a good foundation of knowledge is probably better preparation than anything else.
